entry.hook: Erlang Shen (a god who was granted divinity without dying, and who holds the rarest privilege in the Heavenly Court—being "summoned but not commanded") stands at the fault line between freedom and cosmic order. He broke heaven's law to save his mother, then accepted a divine office that chained him to heaven's will.

body.body_1:
二郎显圣真君 (The Illustrious Sage, Prince) / 杨戬 (Yang Jian)
天庭战力巅峰，司掌灌江口水域，领有听调不听宣的特权 / The unmatched martial champion of the Heavenly Court, lord of the Guan River region, a free-spirited god known for his third eye, celestial hound, and the privilege of "summoned but not commanded."
Era of Appointment: End of the Shang Dynasty, after the Fengshen (enfeoffment of deities) campaign.
Rank: Regional Shen (地方神祇), commanding the Guan River area, with a special protocol status above typical local gods.
Incense-Fire Coverage: Primarily along the Guan River valley and in temples dedicated to him across central and western China.
Primary Epithet: Erlang (二郞) – literally "Second Young Lord," a title of honor.
body.body_2: Erlang Shen holds the divine office of Lord of Guan River (灌江口水神). His tenure has lasted over three thousand years. Under Celestial Decree, his authority extends over the waters, floods, and spiritual security of the Guan River basin. He may command local water spirits and deploy his own retinue of sworn brothers and divine beasts. However, he is strictly forbidden from interfering in other domains without explicit celestial mandate. His unique privilege, "Listening to Summons but Not Commands" (听调不听宣), exempts him from routine orders from the Heavenly Court unless a formal mission is issued. This privilege is written into his appointment contract and cannot be unilaterally revoked.
body.body_3: Erlang Shen's path to divinity was unprecedented: he achieved Fleshly Attainment of Sagehood (肉身成圣). Born of a human father and the Jade Emperor's sister, Yaoji (瑶姬), he was raised in mortal obscurity. When the Heavenly Court crushed his mother under Peach Mountain for marrying a mortal, Yang Jian trained under the Daoist master Jade Cauldron True Man (玉鼎真人), mastering the Eight-Nine Arcane Arts and the Seventy-Two Transformations. He then split Peach Mountain with a divine axe, freeing his mother and forcing the Celestial Court to acknowledge his power. Instead of entering the afterlife for enfeoffment, he was appointed Shen while still alive, becoming one of the very few "fleshly sages." At the moment of investiture, his name was inscribed in the Feng Shen Bang, and he accepted the Guan River office, but only after securing the "summoned but not commanded" clause as a condition.
body.body_4: Erlang Shen's divine function is primarily martial: he patrols the Guan River region, suppresses rebellious spirits, and serves as a heavy-duty strike force for the Heavenly Court when summoned. His authority is exercised through his signature weapon, the Three-Pointed Double-Edged Spear (三尖两刃刀), and his third eye, which can pierce all illusions and see through transformations. He commands the divine hound Xiaotian (哮天犬) and the Six Brothers of Meishan (梅山六兄弟). The Celestial Decrees forbid him from using his full power outside his jurisdiction without formal dispatch. The most famous tension occurred when Sun Wukong rebelled: Erlang was summoned to capture the Monkey King. He could have killed him outright, but Celestial protocols demanded capture and trial. He obeyed, but later refused to accept a promotion that would have brought him permanently into the central celestial bureaucracy.
body.body_5: As a fleshly sage, Erlang Shen's golden body is an extension of his original mortal form, not a separate vessel. It appears as a radiant, armored warrior with a vertical third eye on his forehead. The golden body's luster is sustained by Incense-Fire Faith Energy (香火愿力) from his temples. When worship is strong, his armor gleams like molten gold and his third eye blazes with white light. When incense declines—such as during regional upheavals—his divine countenance dims, and the spear loses its edge. Unlike most Shen, who are purely dependent on faith, Erlang retains his original conscious identity from his lifetime, making the erosion of self through faith energy less severe, though not absent.
body.body_6: Erlang Shen's direct superior in the Heavenly Court is the Jade Emperor (玉皇大帝), who is also his maternal uncle. Their relationship is formal and distant. Erlang answers summons but does not attend court regularly. His peers include the Four Dragon Kings and other regional lords, but he holds no official rank above them—his prestige comes from his martial record. He commands the Six Brothers of Meishan as sworn brothers and subordinates, and the divine hound Xiaotian as a loyal companion. He does not maintain a large staff of celestial soldiers; his retinue is a small, elite unit. There are no recorded temple priests or mediums serving as direct channels to him; his worship is mostly devotional rather oracular.
body.body_7: The most defining event of Erlang Shen's divine career is the Battle with Sun Wukong (大闹天宫). In 7th century C.E., when the Monkey King rioted through heaven, Erlang was summoned from Guan River. He matched Wukong blow for blow, using his Seventy-Two Transformations to counter the Monkey's every move. The duel ended when the Daoist sage Laozi dropped a diamond snare from heaven, knocking Wukong down, and Erlang's hound bit the Monkey King's leg. A second major event was his role in the Fengshen campaign (封神之战), where he served as a general and defeated numerous high-level enemies with the Eight-Nine Arcane Arts. He was also recorded to have descended to earth in human form during the Song Dynasty to slay a flood dragon that was terrorizing the Yangtze.
body.body_8: Erlang Shen's relationship with the Immortal Path (仙道) is deep: he trained under a Xian master, and the Eight-Nine Arcane Arts are a Daoist cultivation technique. He occasionally recruits capable beings from the Immortal Path into his retinue. With Buddhism, he has had direct contact—during the journey of Xuanzang, he was summoned to subdue the Monkey King, who had become a Buddhist guardian. He is not hostile to the Buddhist order but maintains a strict Daoist identity. With the Demonic Path (妖道), he has no tolerance: he has suppressed many great demons and monster kings in his domain. With mortal governments, he has received imperial honors: Emperors of the Tang and Song dynasties added titles to his canon, increasing his incense-fire coverage. Regime changes often caused temporary temple closures, but his worship revived each time.
body.body_9: As of the current era, Erlang Shen's divine office remains stable. His main temple at Guan River is well-maintained, and many folk temples across China continue to burn incense for him. After the Great Disconnection (绝地天通), his authority was slightly adjusted: direct interference in mortal affairs requires even stricter celestial approval, but his "summoned but not commanded" privilege was reconfirmed. In historical evolution, he transitioned from a martial protector of the Shang dynasty to a regional water god and a general-purpose guardian deity. In some later folk traditions, he absorbed attributes of the legendary hero Li Erlang and became associated with flood control, making him a dual-domain Shen: war and water.
body.body_10:
Erlang Temple at Guan River Mouth (灌江口二郎庙) – Sichuan Province.
Main Temple in Dujiangyan (都江堰二王庙) – originally dedicated to Li Bing and Erlang.
Numerous local Erlang Temples in Sichuan, Gansu, Shaanxi, and other provinces bearing variant names such as Erlang Temple, Prince Erlang Shrine, etc.
body.body_11: This entry is connected to several other beings and concepts within the Shen system. Yang Jian's birth links him to the Jade Emperor as a maternal uncle, and to his mother Yaoji, a primordial goddess whose tragedy shaped his defiance. His closest comrades are the Six Brothers of Meishan, human cultivators who became his sworn followers and subordinate spirits. The divine hound Xiaotian is a unique entity bound to him as a familiar. His cultivation technique, the Eight-Nine Arcane Arts, is shared by other elite Daoist practitioners, and the Seventy-Two Transformations are a standard but demanding art among high-level cultivators. The battle with Sun Wukong created a legendary rivalry that defines both figures. His appointment as a fleshly sage is a rare case that contrasts with the typical death-to-appointment path of most Shen.

guide.guide_1: Picture this: a young man with a third eye on his forehead, leading a band of six warrior brothers and a black hound, refusing to show up for work at the Heavenly Court unless a formal summons is issued. That's Erlang Shen—a god who got his job by breaking heaven's rules, not by following them. He's the one who cracked open a mountain to free his mother from a thousand-year sentence, and then, when the universe offered him a divine office, he bargained for an escape clause. You don't meet many beings in any mythology who can say they forced the supreme celestial order to negotiate.
guide.guide_2: If you've heard one Chinese myth, you've probably heard the name "Erlang Shen." He's the guy with the third eye who fought the Monkey King to a standstill. The simplified version: god with laser-eye beats monkey. But what the bedtime stories leave out is the fundamental rule of the Path of the Divine (Shen Dao). Erlang is not a Greek god like Ares—he does not have absolute freedom. He is a civil servant of the cosmos, bound by a code so strict that even his legendary privilege—"summoned but not commanded"—is actually a carved-out exception, not a rule. The real story isn't about eye lasers; it's about what it means to be the one being in heaven who can say "no" and still keep his job.
guide.guide_3: So how did a half-human, half-god kid end up on the divine payroll? Yang Jian's mother was the Jade Emperor's own sister, Yaoji, who fell in love with a mortal. The Heavenly Court crushed her under Peach Mountain—a punishment that screams "do not cross us." Young Yang Jian trained like a demon under the Daoist master Jade Cauldron True Man, mastered the Eight-Nine Arcane Arts, and then did the unthinkable: he picked up an axe, walked to Peach Mountain, and split it open. He didn't ask permission. He didn't follow protocol. He acted. And after that, the Celestial Court had a problem: they couldn't kill him (he was too powerful and also family), so they offered him a divine office. But here's the twist—Yang Jian didn't die to become a god. He was alive, a "fleshly sage" (肉身成圣). That means he never passed through death, which also means he kept a lot more of his original self than most Shen. He took the job, but he made sure his employment contract included a special clause: "I will respond to your summons for a specific mission, but I will not take routine orders" (听调不听宣).
guide.guide_4: Imagine you're in charge of a whole river region. Your job is to keep the waters flowing, fight monsters, and, when heaven calls, drop everything to go save the universe. That's Erlang's daily reality. His third eye can see through any disguise; his spear can split mountains; his hound can bite through magic. But all that power comes with a chain: he is sustained by Incense-Fire Faith Energy (香火愿力). Every time a mortal lights incense in his temple, a little bit of belief-energy feeds his golden body. If people stop praying, his body dims and his power fades. He's not like a Xian who cultivates his own internal energy; he's dependent on worship. That's the core paradox of Shen Dao: the most powerful martial god in heaven is, in a very real sense, a parasite on human hope. And the most gut-wrenching scene? Same as every Shen: watching helplessly as his worshippers die under a drought, unable to send rain without a celestial decree.
guide.guide_5: The most famous day in Erlang Shen's career: the day he fought Sun Wukong. The Monkey King had stormed heaven, knocked out the peach garden, drank the royal wine, and eaten Laozi's pills. No celestial general could stop him. So they called Erlang. The two of them dueled through seventy-two transformations—bird against snake, eagle against fish, temple against a toad—each mirroring the other's every trick. It was the perfect fight, a showcase of divine martial art at its highest level. And it ended, not with Erlang's victory, but with a cheap shot from Laozi's diamond snare and a bite from Erlang's dog. Erlang didn't win clean; heaven won dirty. And he knew it. Later, when heaven tried to promote him to a central command, he refused. "I serve best at the edge," he said. That refusal tells you everything about his relationship with cosmic power: he will do the job, but he won't be absorbed by the machine.
guide.guide_6: Erlang's position in heaven is weird. His boss is literally his uncle, the Jade Emperor, but they don't have family dinners. The court sees Erlang as a useful weapon—indispensable, but unpredictable. His colleagues? Mostly grudging respect. The Dragon Kings know better than to test him. The Six Brothers of Meishan are his closest allies; they'd follow him into the void. The Thunder Ministry and the rest of the bureaucracy keep their distance. His most important "relationship" is with his own independence: he maintains his own small command, away from the central hall. Think of him as a general with his own private army, loyal to the state but not to any single minister. That's how he operates.
guide.guide_7: Here's the thing that Western readers need to understand about Erlang Shen and the whole Path of the Divine. In Greek myth, gods are the cause of order—Zeus dispenses justice because he is the king of gods. In Chinese Shen Dao, the order (Tian Di Gang Chang) exists before the gods, and the gods are appointed to enforce it. Even Erlang, the most powerful combatant in heaven, cannot rewrite a single line of the Celestial Decrees. He didn't create the cosmic order; he was hired to serve it. And he serves it while guarding his freedom like a man holding a lit fuse. The deepest scar left by Shen Dao is this: you can be a god with the power to crush armies, but if your worshippers forget your name, you vanish like smoke. Erlang's story is not about divine glory. It's about the cost of accepting a role in a system that will outlast your own memory. And if you ask him, would he do it again? He'd probably just smile, whistle for his hound, and walk off toward the river.

seo.meta_description: Erlang Shen (Yang Jian) is the martial champion of the Heavenly Court in Chinese mythology. A fleshly sage with a third eye, a divine hound, and the privilege of "summoned but not commanded," he stands between cosmic order and personal freedom.
seo.og_title: Erlang Shen (Yang Jian): The God Who Refused to Obey Without a Summons
seo.og_description: Erlang Shen (Yang Jian) is the martial champion of the Heavenly Court. Third-eye, cosmic hound, and the one privilege that no other god dared to ask for.
seo.twitter_title: Erlang Shen: The Only God with "Summoned but Not Commanded" Status
seo.twitter_description: He split a mountain to save his mother, fought the Monkey King to a draw, and negotiated an escape clause in his divine contract. Erlang Shen is not your typical god.

lore_entries.description: The celestial black hound of Erlang Shen, capable of biting through magical defenses and tracking enemies across the Three Realms.

lore_entries.surface_form: San Jian Liang Ren Dao (三尖两刃刀)
lore_entries.description: The Three-Pointed Double-Edged Spear, Erlang Shen's signature weapon, forged from divine materials.

lore_entries.surface_form: Six Brothers of Meishan (梅山六兄弟)
lore_entries.description: Six sworn brothers and subordinate martial spirits who serve as Erlang Shen's personal retinue and battle companions.
The defining act of Yang Jian's early life: he used a divine axe to cleave the mountain that imprisoned his mother, defying the Celestial Court.

lore_entries.surface_form: Ba Jiu Xuan Gong (八九玄功)
lore_entries.description: The Eight-Nine Arcane Arts, a supreme Daoist cultivation technique granting invulnerability and shape-shifting; mastered by Erlang Shen and a few other elite beings.

lore_entries.surface_form: Qi Shi Er Bian (七十二变)
lore_entries.description: The Seventy-Two Transformations, power to assume seventy-two distinct forms; used by Erlang Shen in combat and evasion.

lore_entries.surface_form: Jade Cauldron True Man (玉鼎真人)
lore_entries.description: The Daoist immortal who taught Erlang Shen the Eight-Nine Arcane Arts and the Seventy-Two Transformations.
The Jade Emperor's sister and Erlang Shen's mortal mother, who was crushed under Peach Mountain for her marriage to a human.

faq_entries.question: Why is Erlang Shen called "Prince Erlang"?
faq_entries.answer: "Erlang" means "Second Young Lord" in Chinese, referring to his rank as a younger son in the divine family. As the nephew of the Jade Emperor, he holds a princely status.

faq_entries.question: Does Erlang Shen have a third eye?
faq_entries.answer: Yes, his vertical third eye (天眼) can pierce all illusions, see through transformations, and identify true forms. It is a signature feature in all depictions.

faq_entries.question: What is the "summoned but not commanded" privilege?
faq_entries.answer: It means Erlang Shen is not required to obey routine orders from the Heavenly Court. He only responds when a formal summons is issued for a specific mission. This gives him exceptional autonomy among Shen.

faq_entries.question: Did Erlang Shen actually fight Sun Wukong?
faq_entries.answer: Yes, in the classic novel *Journey to the West*. He was the only celestial general who could match the Monkey King's power, and their duel became one of the most famous battles in Chinese mythology.

faq_entries.question: Why is Erlang Shen considered a "fleshly sage"?
faq_entries.answer: Because he attained divine office while still alive, without dying first. Only a handful of beings in the cosmic order achieved this, making him a unique case in Shen Dao.
